headline: Tonight's frontal rain stays light and Sunday's showers have dropped out of the models; the first of Tuesday's rain now shows up late Tuesday afternoon, after the 9.5 ft high tide, with the Coastal Flood Warning from 6 AM Monday.

summary.text: Sunday afternoon's shower round is gone: RRFS fell from 0.20 to 0.02 in for its wettest 3 hours and NBM from 0.12 to 0.04 in. Consensus down from 0.13 to 0.04 in.
Wettest 3 hours, next 72 h: HRRR 0.11, GFS 0.11, NBM 0.04, ECMWF 0.04, RRFS 0.02 in. HRRR's 0.11 in comes from one 8 PM hour tonight that RRFS, NBM and ECMWF don't support.
No street flooding expected through Tuesday afternoon. Yellow (garage) needs about 0.71 in in 3 hours or a 0.40 in hour; the wettest hour in any model is 0.11 in.
Light frontal rain this evening, roughly 6 to 9 PM, ending around midnight. Sunday and Monday mostly dry. Tuesday's rain starts late afternoon in ECMWF and NBM and continues into Wednesday.

Tides running about 0.9 to 1.4 ft above prediction. Monday's 9.2 ft high at 10:20 AM runs about 10.5 ft. Tuesday's first rain falls after the 11:02 AM high, on the falling tide. Channel low: 0.15 ft at Alameda.
Nothing needed tonight or Sunday. Use dry Monday: clear street drain grates and yard drains, check sandbags, and plan where cars go for Tuesday night and Wednesday.

sections.title: Synopsis
sections.text: A weakening cold front is moving down from the North Bay and reaches the SF Bay Area this evening (NWS San Francisco, 12:19 PM). NWS notes the high-resolution models disagree on how fast the rain band falls apart: RRFS breaks it into scattered showers over the Bay Area tonight, while HRRR keeps it together. Post-frontal showers remain possible Sunday afternoon and evening, mainly offshore and along the coast. Monday is mainly dry and, per NWS, the day to prepare. Tuesday and Wednesday bring an impactful storm, though NWS trimmed it today: a weaker moisture tap, with a best estimate of 0.5 to 1.5 in of rain for the Bay Area outside the North Bay (more toward the coastal ranges) and gusts mostly 20 to 30 mph. Thanksgiving looks generally dry, with another chance of rain late Friday into the weekend and the storm door staying open into early December.

sections.title: What changed and model trends
sections.text:
Since this morning's discussion, the Sunday shower signal has collapsed and Tuesday's storm has started to enter the model data. Wettest 3 hours / total in the next 72 hours:
• HRRR (2 PM Sat run, ends 10 AM Mon): 0.11 / 0.13 in, wettest 3 hours this evening about 6 to 9 PM, nearly all of it in one 0.11 in hour near 8 PM. Its 15-minute output puts about 0.08 in between 8:00 and 8:30 PM, then only a trace. This morning it had 0.10 in, so little change.
• GFS: 0.11 / 0.13 in, identical to HRRR hour for hour, so it adds little independent support.
• NBM: 0.04 / 0.16 in, light rain this evening (0.03 in in the 9 PM hour), then a slow start to Tuesday's rain from late morning. This morning it had 0.12 in on Sunday afternoon.
• ECMWF: 0.04 / 0.08 in, very light rain this evening, then Tuesday's rain from mid-afternoon.
• RRFS (10 AM Sat run): 0.02 / 0.02 in, down from 0.20 in this morning. It now scatters tonight's band into almost nothing and has no Sunday showers.

Consensus (HRRR 0.11 × 1.25 = 0.14, RRFS 0.02, NBM 0.04): about 0.04 in, down from 0.13 in. HRRR's 8 PM hour is a single isolated cell that only its own lookalike GFS supports, so treat it as a low-confidence shower rather than a trend. Even with HRRR's history of under-forecasting bursts by about 3×, it would be near 0.33 in in 3 hours, under the 0.71 in Yellow threshold.

Tuesday (just past the 72-hour window, data through 11 PM Tue): ECMWF has 0.30 in for Tuesday with its wettest 3 hours 0.18 in from about 5 to 8 PM; NBM 0.42 in with 0.14 in over the same hours; RRFS reaches 0.09 in in the 10 PM hour at the end of its run; GFS stays dry through Tuesday evening. The heavier part of the storm, Tuesday night into Wednesday, is still beyond this snapshot.

sections.title: Tide and the channel
sections.text:
NOAA's Bay model runs about 0.9 to 1.4 ft above the predicted tides at Redwood City, similar to this morning. Tonight's rain falls on the rising tide toward the 6.6 ft high at 10:19 PM (about 8.1 ft on the model around 11 PM), which slows drainage late this evening, but the amounts are small. Sunday's 8.8 ft high at 9:42 AM runs about 10.2 ft. The model now reaches Monday: the 9.2 ft high at 10:20 AM runs about 10.5 ft, the highest so far this cycle. Tuesday's 9.5 ft high at 11:02 AM is past the model's end (1 PM Monday). In ECMWF and NBM, Tuesday's first meaningful rain arrives in the late afternoon, on the falling tide toward the -1.5 ft low at 6:28 PM, which is good for drainage; Wednesday's late-morning high is the overlap to watch once the data reach it.

NWS reissued the coastal products at 2:30 PM: the Coastal Flood Advisory runs until 6 AM Monday, then the Coastal Flood Warning (up to 2.8 ft of inundation in low-lying areas near shorelines and tidal waterways) through 4 PM Thursday. NWS now expects San Francisco high tides 2.6 ft above normal Tuesday and 2.8 ft Wednesday (this morning: 2.9 and 3.0 ft), including up to 1.6 ft of surge, still approaching the highest tide ever recorded. High tides with surge slow the channel's drainage.

Channel: at Alameda de las Pulgas it reads 0.15 ft at 4 PM, flat all day (Flood Monitoring 3.18 ft). The gauge upstream of Caltrain last reported at 5:13 AM, 0.07 ft (Flood Monitoring 2.8 ft), about 11 hours ago.

sections.title: Current observations
sections.text: Dry so far today under high clouds. The Caltrain rain gauge showed 0.00 in over the 24 hours to its last report at 5:13 AM; there is no newer local rain reading. The Alameda channel gauge is low and steady.

sections.title: Uncertainty
sections.text: Low through Monday: four of five models keep the wettest 3 hours at 0.11 in or less, and the only question tonight is whether HRRR's coherent band or RRFS's scattered showers verify. Neither reaches flooding amounts. Tuesday and Wednesday carry the real uncertainty: NWS trimmed rainfall today, the models disagree on when steady rain starts (GFS later than ECMWF and NBM), and the heaviest rain and its overlap with Wednesday's late-morning king tide are not yet in this snapshot.

sections.title: What to do
sections.text:
• No need to move cars tonight or Sunday.
• Monday (dry, before the warning-level tides and Tuesday's rain): clear leaves from street drain grates and yard drains, check sandbags, and decide where cars will go Tuesday night and Wednesday if the rain lands near a high tide. Power outages from Tuesday's wind can slow the pumps.
• Stay away from the Bay shore and tidal sloughs at the morning high tides; don't walk or drive through moving water.
